subtitleEn: Talk at the table with a family cooking together.
hoyaIntroEn: Something smells good! Let us join the family in the kitchen.

quests.blurbEn: Answer a warm hello at the family table.
quests.teaserEn: Next: ask how the food tastes.

steps.hoyaLineEn: Grandma asks if we have eaten. It is her way of saying hello!

pages.captionEn: Asking if someone has eaten is a warm hello that shows care.
The past ending tells about something already done: eaten, drunk.

steps.hoyaLineEn: You answered a warm hello at the table!

replies.whyEn: That one is for a drink. Grandma asks about a meal, so say you ate.
That tells your name. Grandma is asking if you ate: a warm hello.
Kimchi is food, so say you ate it.
That is a goodbye. Grandma asked about the kimchi, so answer her.
Milk is a drink, so pick the answer that says you drank it.
That asks for an apple. Grandma asked about your milk.

line.en: Did you eat the rice cake?

replies.whyEn: Rice cake is food, so say you ate it.
That is for meeting someone new. Grandma asked about the rice cake.

nodes.closingEn: You answered every warm question at the table!

line.en: Did you eat the rice cake?

quests.blurbEn: Ask how the food is, and answer.
quests.teaserEn: Next: is it spicy? Say yes or no.

steps.hoyaLineEn: Dinner is ready. Let us ask how everything tastes!

pages.captionEn: Name the thing, then ask how it is. The answer can be one word.

steps.hoyaLineEn: You asked how the food tastes. Yum!

replies.whyEn: Dad asks if you have eaten, not how it tastes. Say you ate.
That asks a question back. Dad asked you, so answer him.
Dad asks how it tastes, not if you ate. Tell him how it is.
That is a goodbye. Dad asks how it tastes, so tell him.
That says you drank something. Dad asks how the kimchi is.
That tells your name. Dad asks how the kimchi is.
That only says you drank something. Dad asks how the apple is.
That asks for an apple. Dad asks how the apple is.

nodes.closingEn: You told Dad how everything tastes. Time to eat!

quests.blurbEn: Say that something is not spicy or not hot.

steps.hoyaLineEn: Is it spicy? Let us find out, and say no if it is not!

pages.captionEn: To say not, put the short word for not just before the describing word.

steps.hoyaLineEn: You said yes and no at the family table!

replies.whyEn: That asks a question back. Mom asks if it is spicy, so say yes or no.
That says you drank it. Mom asks if it is spicy, so say yes or no.
Mom asks if the soup is hot, not if it is spicy.
That says you drank it. Mom asks if the soup is hot.
Mom asks about spice, not about heat.
That is a goodbye. Mom asks if the kimchi is spicy.
Mom asks how it tastes, not a yes-or-no question. Tell her how it is.
That tells your name. Mom asks how it tastes.

nodes.closingEn: You said yes and no at the family table!

culture.textEn: People often ask {ko:밥 먹었어요?} as a friendly hello. It shows care, and a short answer is enough.

sources.title: 인사예절 (한류문화사전)
sources.publisher: 국립민속박물관 (National Folk Museum of Korea) — 한국민속대백과사전
sources.quoteOrLocator: 내용, 2. 언어 인사예절 ⑦: ‘전통적인 인사언어로는 ‘밥 먹었니?’ ‘식사하셨습니까?’ ‘진지 잡수셨습니까?’ 등이 있다.’ / ‘식사 여부를 묻는 것이 안부를 확인하는 보통의 인사로 정착한 것으로 보인다.’

sources.title: 인사, an entry of the Encyclopedia of Korean Culture
sources.publisher: 한국민족문화대백과사전 (Encyclopedia of Korean Culture), Academy of Korean Studies
sources.quoteOrLocator: Entry 인사, section 내용, (1) 말로 하는 인사, ①: “아침식사 뒤에는 ‘진지 자셨나？’, ‘밥 먹었는가？’ … 등으로 인사말을 나눈다.” and “우리의 평상시 인사말은 취식여부(取食與否)와 신변안부에 관한 물음으로 되어 있다. 이러한 인사말은 오늘날에도 변함없이 교환되고 있다.” Definition: “안부를 묻거나 공경·친애·우정의 뜻을 표시하는 예의.”

sources.title: “언제 밥이나 한번 먹죠” (Let us have a meal sometime), a personal opinion column by Han Gi-bong
sources.publisher: 대한민국 정책브리핑 (Korea Policy Briefing), korea.kr, opinion section; the author's own view
sources.quoteOrLocator: Column of 2018-08-31: “‘밥 먹었어요?’처럼 그냥 인사치레다.” and “시골에 사는 노모가 전화로 ‘밥은 먹었나?’하면 … 질문이 아니라 관심과 애정의 표현이라는 걸 알기 때문이다.”

sources.title: 국립민속박물관 속 전통문화, 오늘의 K-컬처로 이어지다 (Traditional culture in the National Folk Museum of Korea continues into today's K-culture)
sources.publisher: 대한민국 정책브리핑 (Korea Policy Briefing), korea.kr, 정책기자단 citizen-reporter piece; the wording is the reporter's
sources.quoteOrLocator: Report of 2025-11-13, on the museum's section <함께 하는>: “식탁을 함께 둘러앉아 ‘밥 먹었어?’ 라고 묻는 평범한 인사 …”

sources.title: 표준 언어 예절(2011) - 일상생활의 인사말 (Standard Language Etiquette, chapter IV: everyday greetings)
sources.quoteOrLocator: Chapter IV, section 19 만나고 헤어질 때의 인사말, p. 172: “식사 시간 무렵에 동년배나 아랫사람을 만났을 때는 ‘식사하셨습니까?’, ‘식사하셨어요?’, ‘식사했어요?’, ‘점심 먹었어요?’ 등과 같이 인사할 수 있다.” Table IV-5 (p. 173), 식사 시간 전후에 만났을 때: ‘점심/진지 잡수셨습니까?’, ‘점심/진지 드셨습니까?’, ‘식사하셨어요?’, ‘점심/밥 먹었어?’.

verification.notes:
Line 1 (pass 2, author sourcing, 2026-10-14): both pages fetched; the column calls the question a customary greeting and an expression of care rather than a real question; the 정책기자단 citizen-reporter piece on an NFMK exhibit (the reporter's wording) describes it as an ordinary greeting at a shared table. The note says 'often', names no group as a whole and copies no wording. Carried by: q1 intro Hoya line and q1 Discover page 1 caption.
Line 2 (pass 2b, independent fact check by a separate session, 2026-10-14): both korea.kr pages re-fetched; every quoteOrLocator passage found on its page (column dated 2018-08-31 calls the question just a customary greeting and, in the mother's phone call, care and affection rather than a real question; report dated 2025-11-13 describes asking it around the shared table as an ordinary greeting as the reporter describes the museum's third section). 'Family and friends often ask' is supported (family in both, closeness between acquaintances in the column); 'shows care' is supported; 'a short answer is enough' follows from both pages calling it a greeting rather than a real question. The note and the carrying lines are original English and copy no source wording; host www.korea.kr is on the allowlist; no group-wide claim, stereotype, living person, shop, brand or price. Outcome: kept unchanged.
Line 3 (pass 5, MAR culture review, final independent fact check, 2026-10-14): the review found both korea.kr sources were private writing on a public host (an opinion column and a citizen-reporter piece), not an institution's own statement, so the AKS Encyclopedia of Korean Culture entry 인사 was added as the institutional source; all three pages re-fetched and every quoteOrLocator passage found. The entry lists asking whether someone has eaten among everyday greetings still exchanged today and defines a greeting as asking after someone and showing warmth. 'Family and friends' was narrowed to 'People often ask'. Source labels in lines 1-2 corrected. No copied wording, no group-wide claim, stereotype, living person, shop, brand or price. Outcome: changed as stated, passes 3.
CM-3C (2026-10-23): culture-source fix. The National Folk Museum of Korea entry 인사예절 (Hallyu culture dictionary, topic 12123) added first: asking whether someone has eaten (밥 먹었니?) is a traditional greeting that asks after the person. The note's words are unchanged; the short answer stays with the korea.kr column.

notes: Language (pass 4, MAR): q2 no longer asks a q3 word before q3 teaches it; English glosses name the verb (Yes, I ate / Yes, I drank it); ko captions fixed (상태를 나타내는 말, 말끝); q1 Apply has 4 lines; yes/no wording uses 네/아니요.

Culture (pass 5, MAR): AKS Encyclopedia of Korean Culture source added for the have-you-eaten greeting, note narrowed to People often ask; source labels corrected; spicy turn moved from kimchi to this soup; elder lines in 해요체 kept as polite models.

Check rotation MAR (row CM-3A S4, F-CURR-002 section 7.1, 2026-10-27; passes: language, culture and facts, learning design, reviser, third pass): Food plays Role Play (Grandma, Dad and Mom at home, 4 turns each, every branch ends well) and Sentence Builder with particle choices; the Checks are Dialogue reply pick (Tap to Respond), Cloze Pick and Dialogue reply pick.

CM-3A S4 MAR (cont.): Language: one natural reply per turn, so a less natural reply is never a second right answer; 'No' never answers a how question; 사과가 after a vowel, 국이 and 맛이 after a final consonant; elders speak 해요체, kept as polite models. Culture and facts: no new claim; the have-you-eaten note and its source are unchanged.

CM-3A S4 MAR (cont.): Learning design: the Role Plays, Builders and Checks re-ask the cell's own exchanges and sentences (one new turn, the rice cake, and three new sentences), so the review load stays under the section 4.3 gate. Reviser and third pass: es and ko overlays checked; no native-speaker or expert review is claimed.
